title: Main Topic of Informational Texts
keyIdea: A fact book or page has a main topic: the one thing every sentence tells about. Facts that tell about the topic are key details; things someone likes are not. You can say the main topic in one sentence, retell a few key facts, and use words like so to show how two facts are linked.

kid: A fact page tells you about one big thing. That is the main topic. Ask: what does every sentence tell about?
Owls hunt at night. Owls have big eyes. Owls eat mice. Mice are in it, but just once. Every sentence is about owls. So the main topic is owls.
Key facts teach you about the topic. "Plants need water" is a key fact. "I like sunflowers best" is not. It just says what someone likes.
Some facts are linked. It rained all day, so the river got high. The word so shows how one thing made the next thing happen.
adult: Informational texts, such as fact books about animals or space, are organised around a main topic. At five to seven, children learn to say what a short text is mostly about in one sentence, to list two or three key facts they learned, and to explain how two facts or events are connected, often by cause and effect.

The lab builds each skill with its own action. Children tap a word to see which sentences tell about it, sort facts into a shark book, pick the one sentence that sums up a page, choose key facts about plants while leaving out opinions, and link pairs of facts with so.

Common mistakes to watch for: naming a detail that is vivid or comes last, such as mice on an owl page, as the topic; accepting a fact because it is near the topic, such as dolphins in a shark book; giving one fact as a summary; and treating opinions or personal stories as key details. Pronouns can also hide the topic, so check what they or it points back to.
To help, after reading a page together, ask: "What was every sentence about?" then "Tell me two things you learned." Use the title and pictures as clues, but check them against the sentences.

familyTip: After reading a non-fiction page or a cereal box together, ask, "What was it all about?" and "Tell me two things you learned." Then ask how two facts are linked: "It was cold, so what happened?"

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find what every sentence is about, sort facts into a shark book, pick a one-sentence summary, choose key facts and link facts with so.

practice.prompt: A page says: Ants live in big groups. Ants dig tunnels. Ants carry food home. What is the main topic?
practice.hint: What does every sentence tell about?
practice.explain: Every sentence tells about ants. Tunnels and food are details about the ants.

practice.prompt: A fact book about the moon has {n} pages. Which fact belongs in it?
choices: The moon goes round the Earth.
practice.hint: A fact belongs when it tells about the topic of the book.
practice.explain: Only the first fact tells about the moon, so it belongs in all {n} pages of the moon book.

practice.prompt: Which is a key fact about how fish breathe?
choices: Fish use gills to take air from water.
practice.hint: A key fact teaches about the topic. It is not what someone likes or owns.
practice.explain: Gills taking air from water is the fact that teaches how fish breathe. The others are about someone.

practice.prompt: It snowed for {n} days. Which is the best way to link it to the next fact?
practice.hint: Pick what snow could make happen.
practice.explain: After {n} days of snow, the roads were white. Snow does not make it hot, and jam has no link.

pool.prompt: A page says: Bats sleep in the day. Bats fly at night. They eat bugs. What is it about?
pool.hint: Who is "they"? What does every sentence tell about?
pool.explain: They means bats, so every sentence tells about bats. Bugs are one detail.

pool.prompt: Which sentence sums up a page about how a chick hatches?
choices: This page is about how a chick hatches.
pool.hint: A summary tells about the whole page, not one detail.
pool.explain: The first sentence covers the whole page. Fluffy is one detail, and farms is too wide.

pool.prompt: A book about cars has {n} facts. One says "Bikes have two wheels." Does it belong?
pool.hint: Ask: is this fact about cars, or something else?
pool.explain: Bikes are close to cars, but the fact tells about bikes, so it does not belong with the {n} car facts.

pool.prompt: Is "My dog is the best" a key fact for a page about how dogs smell things?
choices: No, it is what someone thinks
pool.hint: Does it teach how dogs smell things?
pool.explain: It says what someone thinks. It does not teach how dogs smell, so it is not a key fact.

pool.prompt: You read a page with {n} facts about sharks. How many key facts might you retell?
pool.hint: A retell gives a few of the most useful facts.
pool.explain: Pick two or three key facts from the {n} to retell. You do not need all of them, but you need some.

pool.prompt: The sun came out. The ice melted. Which word links them?
pool.hint: Did the sun make the ice melt?
pool.explain: The sun made the ice melt, so we use so: the sun came out, so the ice melted.

pool.prompt: A page says: Owls hunt at night. Owls eat mice. Owls have big eyes. A child says it is about mice. What went wrong?
pool.hint: How many sentences tell about mice?
pool.explain: Mice is in one sentence. Every sentence tells about owls, so owls is the main topic.
